title: Given the root of a binary tree, invert it so that the left and right children of every node are swapped, producing a mirror image of the original tree.
shortTitle: Invert/Mirror Binary Tree: swap left and right recursively
keyPoints: Inverting a tree swaps the left and right children of every node, producing the mirror image
The base case is a null node, which has nothing to swap and returns null
The order of swap-then-recurse versus recurse-then-swap does not affect the final result
Time is O(n) because every node is visited once; space is O(h) for the recursion stack
An iterative BFS or DFS alternative avoids deep recursion on skewed trees
Decide whether to mutate in place or build a new tree depending on whether the original is still needed

s1_definition.oneliner: At every node swap its two children, then recursively invert both subtrees to produce the mirror image.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Invert Binary Tree** produces the mirror image of a tree by swapping the left and right child at every node.
- **Recursive traversal** visits each node, performs a constant-time swap, and recurses into both children.
- **Order independence** means you can swap first then recurse, or recurse first then swap, with identical results.
- **In-place mutation** modifies the original tree; a non-destructive variant builds a new mirrored tree.
- **Time** is O(n) for one visit per node; **space** is O(h) for the call stack.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has the National Bank of India's approval hierarchy drawn on glass and wants to see how it looks from the other side, as a mirror image. At every manager, the person who was on the left now appears on the right and vice versa. He does this swap at the top, then repeats it for each sub-team all the way down. The result is the same chart flipped left-to-right.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Invert Binary Tree (swap at every node)
  ========================================

  Before:         4               After:         4
                 / \                             / \
                2    7                          7    2
               / \  / \                        / \  / \
              1  3 6   9                      9  6 3   1

  Swap operations (pre-order):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  At node 4: swap(2, 7)          │
  │  At node 7: swap(6, 9)          │
  │  At node 9: swap(null, null)    │
  │  At node 6: swap(null, null)    │
  │  At node 2: swap(1, 3)          │
  │  At node 3: swap(null, null)    │
  │  At node 1: swap(null, null)    │
  └──────────────────────────────────┘

  Logic per node:
  ┌────────────────────┐
  │ null? → return     │
  │ swap left, right   │
  │ recurse(left)      │
  │ recurse(right)     │
  └────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Inverting a binary tree is a transformation rather than a query: you mutate the structure to produce its mirror image. The operation is naturally recursive. At each node you swap its left and right children, then recursively invert both subtrees. The base case is a null node, which has nothing to swap.

An important point for interviews is that the order of swapping versus recursing does not matter. Whether you swap first and then recurse (pre-order) or recurse first and then swap (post-order), every node performs exactly one swap and the final mirrored tree is identical. What matters is that no node is missed and none is swapped twice.

The time is O(n) because every node is visited once with a constant-time swap, and the space is O(h) for the recursion stack. For very deep trees, the iterative version using a queue avoids any stack overflow risk. You should also clarify with the interviewer whether to mutate in place or build a new tree, depending on whether the original is still needed.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in a disaster-recovery drill service. The approval hierarchy stores primary approvers on the left and backups on the right, and the drill needs the mirror version where backups become primary at every level. The recursive swap flips the entire chain consistently, persisted as a drill snapshot so operations can validate backup wiring before a real failover.

Remember one sentence: at every node swap its two children and recurse into both, and the order of swap versus recurse does not matter.
